chunks: Why many capacitors on a power rail. The question: Often times on a power rail, there are many capacitors connected to ground. What are these capacitors and why are there so many?
Why can you just put one massive capacitor?
Those small capacitors next to a chip are decoupling capacitors. They act as little local energy reserves.
A chip pulls current in sharp bursts that the distant regulator cannot supply fast enough. The capacitors cover each burst so the voltage on the rail doesn't dip.
Think of a restaurant kitchen. A big delivery truck (the regulator) is slow to arrive. So each cook keeps a small bowl of ingredients right at the station.
A single huge container across the kitchen would be too far to reach quickly. Many small bowls placed close to each cook work better.
The bowls are the capacitors, placed right at the chip's pins.
The three series elements of a real capacitor.
Reactances omega L and 1 over omega C have opposite signs, so they cancel at one frequency, the SRF; beyond it the part is inductive.
Decoupling capacitor: a capacitor placed close to a chip's supply pins to supply fast current bursts.
ESL: the small unwanted inductance (a resistance to fast changes in current) of a real capacitor and its mounting. ESR: the small unwanted series resistance of a real capacitor.
Self-resonant frequency: above it, a capacitor acts like an inductor. Impedance: how strongly a part opposes changing current at a given frequency.
Suppose one capacitor and its mounting have 5 nanohenries of inductance. At 100 megahertz its inductive impedance is 2 pi times 10 to the 8 times 5 times 10 to the -9 about 3.
1 ohms. Put ten of them in parallel and the inductance divides by ten, giving about 0. 31 ohms. That is ten times lower impedance at that frequency. That is the whole idea.
"They're decoupling capacitors, acting as local charge reservoirs so fast current bursts don't pull the rail down.
There are many because a real capacitor has ESR and inductance, so each one is only a low impedance over a limited band, above its self-resonant frequency it looks like an inductor.
Paralleling several small parts divides the inductance and gives low impedance out to hundreds of megahertz.
One massive capacitor has a big package and long path, so it's inductive exactly where the chip needs help."
